title: Built a pure Rust perp trading bot running on a home server for Hyperliquid - 10 days of real data & lessons learned
author: Kindly_Skill176
selftext:
Hey guys,



Wanted to share a project I’ve been working on for the past couple of weeks. Got tired of Python bots feeling sluggish on WebSocket streams, so I decided to build an autonomous perp trading bot in pure Rust (using tokio) running 24/7 on my home server (OpenMediaVault in Docker) across BTC, ETH, SOL, and AVAX on Hyperliquid.



The strategy is basically a dual-engine setup. One engine does 5m Ornstein-Uhlenbeck mean reversion with Kalman filters to avoid fading waterfalls, and the other does 15m Donchian breakouts with Chandelier trailing stops. A 4D Gaussian HMM handles the regime switching between range-bound, breakout, and neutral cash buffer.



A few practical things I learned running this live:



1. Maker execution makes or breaks the math. On Hyperliquid, taker fees (4.5 bps) plus crossing slippage eat up scalps fast. Routing exclusively as Post-Only (Alo) and stepping 1 tick inside 2-tick spreads gets you queue priority #1 and actually earns rebates.



2. Standard O-U mean reversion is suicidal without multi-bar confirmation. Early on, the bot would try to catch falling knives on the first band touch. I had to add a rule requiring 2 closed 1m bars without new extremes plus a minimum rebound hurdle before placing orders. False entries dropped massively.



3. Sizing and stops: Had a rough start earlier where wins were frequent but a couple of bad trades ate multiple days of profit. Recalibrated the soft invalidation stops to cut trades at -25 to -40 bps max on 5m closes, and set up a profit giveback ratchet at 75% progress. 



Over the last 5 days it took 7 live trades: 6 wins, 1 small loss ($142.18 -> $142.73). Win rate is sitting around 85%, and average win is now bigger than the average loss.



I also added a discrete-event backtester inside the binary that replays the actual 1-minute order book tape we record on the server (over 57k candles now). Replays 10 days of data in under 2 seconds.



The project is fully open source if anyone wants to check out the Rust implementation or run it:

[https://github.com/JoaoSilvaIT/Markov-Polo](https://github.com/JoaoSilvaIT/Markov-Polo)



Happy to answer any questions about the Rust SDK, L2 data handling or the math behind the O-U filter.

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body: 10 days across four coins is mostly one market mood, so the HMM probably hasn't had to earn its keep yet. how many times has it actually flipped regimes since you went live?

replies.author: Kindly_Skill176
replies.body:
Fair point on the 10-day window, but it actually wasn’t just one mood. We had range chop mid-week, a nasty liquidation flush on Oct 26th where ETH printed a -6.5σ shock bar, and then clean trend expansions on Oct 30–31st where SOL and AVAX broke out and trended down 8-10%.

In terms of flips, the controller evaluated around 3,800 15m bars across the four coins and transitioned states a couple dozen times, but the asymmetric dwell prevented it from ping-ponging back and forth. 

BTC was by far the quietest, sitting in Mean Reversion roughly 80% of the time with occasional drops to Neutral cash when volatility expanded. But AVAX and SOL flipped between Mean Reversion, Neutral, and Trend multiple times. In fact, 4 of the 7 live trades over the last few days were Engine B Trend breakouts (which strictly require the HMM to confirm Trend at P\_T > 75% plus a Donchian breakout), like the AVAX long run to $8.59.

Where the HMM really earned its keep was during the Oct 26th flush. It dropped straight into Neutral with a 15m shock cooldown instead of letting the mean-reversion engine try to fade a -6.5σ waterfall. 

Honestly, the biggest value hasn't been flipping between Long and Short constantly, but spending \~35-40% of the time sitting in Neutral cash refusing to take trades when the regime posteriors are split 50/50.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: a couple dozen flips over 3,800 bars is more than I'd have guessed, fair. the bar I'd look at is the Oct 26 flush: an HMM fit on chop and trend tends to file a -6.5σ bar under whichever of the two it sits nearer, and that's the one bar where the label really matters.

comments.author: BuneHops
comments.body: Looks interesting, thanks for sharing here.

comments.author: madrading
comments.body: What does the one-minute order-book tape contain: individual book updates and trades, or a snapshot/candle per minute? I'd validate the replay against your seven live orders before tuning the strategy: compare submission time, time to first fill, filled quantity and cancellation outcome. If the stored data cannot resolve what happened between updates, show a range of fill assumptions rather than one precise queue result. That would help separate a signal problem from an execution-model problem.

replies.author: Kindly_Skill176
replies.body: The 1m tape (hl\_history\_{symbol}.jsonl) stores a composite per-minute record OHLCV, top-of-book bid/ask, continuous EWMA L2 OBI (instant, 1s, 5s computed off the live WebSocket stream), funding, and open interest rather than raw L2 tick-by-tick diffs, specifically to keep NAS storage around \~1 MB/day. Because 1m bars can't resolve sub-minute queue position directly, the backtester supports toggling between optimistic touch-fills (strict\_trade\_through\_fills = false) and conservative 1-tick trade-through fills (strict\_trade\_through\_fills = true) with adaptive intrabar path ordering to bound the execution range, and we cross-check those bounds against our live shadow-vs-real counterfactual log (counterfactual.rs) before touching any model parameters.
